strengths: The problem setting is well-motivated and realistic: delayed outcomes where treatment affects both outcome timing and value ('pull-forward' effects) break the fixed-sequence assumption underlying most anytime-valid methods, and the design-based framing with a calendar-time cumulative reward estimand avoids strong superpopulation or proportional-hazards assumptions.

The characterization in Theorem 4.4 (augmentation must activate at the event time and remain constant thereafter to preserve the martingale property under the single-arm filtration) is a clean, exact result that both explains why naive AIPW fails and enables practical variance reduction via event-time augmentation; the two-directional proof in Appendix A.1 is careful and correct.

The negative result (Proposition 4.8 with Lemma 4.7: the treatment-effect error is not a martingale under any filtration) is a genuinely interesting impossibility statement, and Remark 4.11 gives an insightful, unified explanation connecting the unestimable cross-term in fixed-sample design-based variance to the incompatibility of arm filtrations in the sequential setting.

Proposition 4.12 provides a useful counterpoint to the expected conservatism: the union bound is asymptotically tighter than the variance upper bound under asymmetric variance clocks, with explicit limiting ratios (2√(π(1−π)) and √(1−π)).

Empirical validation covers the essentials: simulation coverage consistent with theory (Table 2, both oracle and estimated variance clocks), clear demonstration of pointwise CI violations under optional stopping (Figure 1), quantified width reductions from event-time AIPW (76–86%), and a real OOM canary case study with a substantive comparison to the Poisson-process approach of Lindon & Kallus (2025), including the point that design-based inference accommodates varying propensities.

The writing is clear and well-organized; the three-filtration taxonomy (designer, observer, single-arm) makes the technical obstacles easy to follow, and the paper is honest that the union bound is conservative, framing it as the sequential analog of the classical variance upper bound.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate: the machinery (strong approximation via Strassen, Gaussian mixture boundaries via Ville's inequality, asymptotic CS definition) is imported almost directly from Waudby-Smith et al. (2024) and Ham et al. (2022); the genuinely new results are Theorem 4.4, the impossibility result, and Proposition 4.12, which are elegant but individually incremental. Theorem 4.9 is a trivial union bound.

The empirical evaluation is thin for a main-track paper: a single synthetic DGP with N=500 units, and no quantitative head-to-head width comparison with competitor methods (e.g., logrank-style tests, the Poisson approach) on the synthetic data; coverage of 100% in several AIPW cells suggests substantial conservatism that is not investigated (e.g., via nonasymptotic alternatives or boundary calibration).

Only asymptotic guarantees are provided, contingent on the strong approximation and the requirement Vt(w) → ∞; no nonasymptotic confidence sequence (e.g., empirical-Bernstein or sub-Gamma boundaries on bounded increments) is offered, which would be more robust for practice in this bounded-outcome setting.

There is a minor looseness between the theorem statement and usage: Theorem 4.4 is stated in terms of per-unit deterministic conditions on m_it(w), but the running-mean augmentation makes m a random quantity depending on other units' assignments; the text patches this via F-measurability, but the theorem statement should accommodate this directly.

The estimand (cumulative reward growing with t, with interval widths that grow rather than shrink) may limit practical appeal for experimenters who want per-unit or average metrics; the paper argues rescaling invariance for detecting separation, but a direct analysis of the rescaled process is not provided.
No code release or reproducibility artifact is mentioned; the simulation is described in enough detail to be reproducible in principle, but the real-data case study cannot be reproduced.

The limitations of the approach (asymptotic-only, conservative in the balanced/symmetric case, sensitivity of the running-mean augmentation under small samples) are discussed only implicitly, and there is no dedicated limitations section.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: anytime-valid inference for randomized experiments where treatment affects both outcome timing and value (the 'pull-forward' effect), a realistic and underexplored setting in the anytime-valid inference literature.

Careful and instructive filtration analysis (Designer, Observer, Single-Arm filtrations, Definitions 4.1–4.3) that precisely isolates why delayed outcomes break standard constructions, and a clean characterization (Theorem 4.4) of exactly which augmentations preserve the martingale property under the single-arm filtration.

The negative result (Lemma 4.7 + Proposition 4.8) that the treatment-effect error process is not a martingale under any filtration is an interesting structural finding, and Remark 4.11 draws a compelling analogy between the union bound in the sequential setting and the variance upper bound in fixed-sample design-based inference.
Proposition 4.12 showing the union bound can be tighter than the variance upper bound under asymmetric variance clocks is a nice, practically relevant observation with a simple but complete proof.

Proofs are included and largely self-contained; the proof of Theorem 4.6 correctly verifies adaptedness of the variance estimator and the o(1) replacement of the oracle variance clock, following the now-standard Waudby-Smith et al. framework.

Honest positioning of the estimand (sample cumulative reward as a function of calendar time) with a thoughtful discussion of why superpopulation and survival-analytic approaches are hard to justify under nonstationarity and staggered entry.
Includes a real production case study (OOM canary testing) with a concrete comparison to the Poisson-based approach of Lindon & Kallus (2025), clarifying design-based vs. model-based uncertainty.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is narrow: a single synthetic data-generating process (N = 500) and one real case study. There is no simulation comparison against the closest baselines, e.g., design-based confidence sequences of Ham et al. (2022) adapted to this setting, anytime-valid logrank-type tests (Gu & Lai, 1991; Ter Schure et al., 2020), or the counting-process approach of Lindon & Kallus (2025) under misspecified hazards. The comparison to Lindon & Kallus is only qualitative, in a case study with no ground truth, so claims of flexibility/tightness relative to alternatives are not empirically substantiated.

The guarantees are asymptotic (asymptotic confidence sequences requiring Vt(w) → ∞, strong approximation on an enriched probability space) rather than nonasymptotic. For a paper whose selling point is minimal-assumption, design-based rigor, the lack of any finite-sample validity result or finite-sample error quantification is a limitation; the simulations use a single configuration and do not probe small-sample behavior.

The main novelty is incremental relative to Ham et al. (2022): the core machinery (mixture martingale boundary, strong approximation, estimated variance clock) is imported nearly wholesale, and the primary new technical content is the filtration analysis and the impossibility result. The latter, while clean, is a relatively direct consequence of the covariance structure of IPW estimators and may strike some readers as expected.

The practical decision value of the estimand deserves more scrutiny. Δt = rt(1) − rt(0) at calendar time t under treatment-dependent censoring patterns is an unusual quantity: as the authors themselves note, which arm is 'better' depends on the horizon, and the paper explicitly defers all decisions to the practitioner without offering any guidance on how the time-indexed inference should be acted upon. The paper would benefit from a more concrete discussion of what actions this supports.

No code or reproducibility materials are mentioned. The synthetic DGP is described in enough detail to reimplement, but the real telemetry data is proprietary and not reproducible; no statement about releasing code is given.

Proposition 4.12 is asymptotic and assumes constant assignment probability π; the tightness claim of the union bound over the variance upper bound is therefore only established in a restricted regime, and the finite-α, finite-V behavior (where the extra log factors matter) is not explored.

Some presentation issues: the running-mean augmentation fi(w) = ȳ (Section 4.1) introduces subtleties (residuals that depend on past assignments) that are handled only in a brief proof sketch in the appendix; and the 'if and only if' in Theorem 4.4 is stated for a specific class of deterministic augmentations, a scope that should be flagged more explicitly in the main text.

strengths: The design-based formulation of delayed outcomes—treating the event time t_i(w) as a potential outcome alongside the value y_i(w)—is a clean and natural way to handle the joint effect of treatment on timing and magnitude, and the resulting calendar-time cumulative-reward estimand is well motivated for online experimentation (avoids survival-analytic extrapolation beyond the censoring horizon).

The filtration analysis is careful and correct: the distinction between designer (G_t), observer (H_t), and single-arm (F_t(w)) filtrations is illuminating, and Theorem 4.4 gives a sharp if-and-only-if characterization of which augmentations preserve the martingale property (activate at event time, constant thereafter). The proof of Theorem 4.4 correctly handles both adaptedness and the zero-mean jump condition, including both failure modes in the converse.

The negative result (Lemma 4.7 + Proposition 4.8) that the treatment-effect error process is not a martingale under any filtration is a genuinely interesting structural finding, and the analogy drawn in Remark 4.11 between the sequential martingale failure and the classical unestimable cross-term/variance upper bound is a thoughtful unifying insight.

Proposition 4.12 provides a concrete and useful justification that the union bound is not merely a conservative fallback: in the asymmetric variance-clock regime it is strictly tighter (limit R_π → √(1−π)) than the variance upper bound, which is the practically relevant regime for pull-forward effects.

The proofs are largely self-contained and correct: the mixture-martingale construction, Ville's inequality application, and the replacement of V_t by V̂_t (including the argument that V̂_t − V_t is a martingale under event-time augmentation) follow standard but nontrivial lines (Waudby-Smith et al., Ham et al.) and are adapted appropriately to the random jump-time structure.

The empirical evaluation validates the theory: coverage of the anytime-valid sequences is at or above nominal across Monte Carlo replications while pointwise intervals clearly fail (red dots in Figure 1), and the event-time AIPW running-mean augmentation yields substantial width reductions (76–86%) over plain IPW.

The real OOM canary case study (Appendix C) demonstrates practical applicability, and the comparison to Lindon & Kallus (2025) clearly articulates when design-based inference is preferable (varying propensities, no Poisson assumption).
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is thin: a single synthetic data-generating process (N=500, one propensity setting) plus one qualitative case study. There is no sensitivity analysis over effect asymmetry, entry rates, delay distributions, or sample sizes, and no comparison of statistical power/width against alternatives in regimes where they are valid (e.g., logrank-style tests under proportional hazards), making it hard to gauge when the proposed method is preferable in practice.

The negative result, while elegant, rests on a standard martingale fact (Lemma 4.7 is a textbook covariance identity), and the proof of Proposition 4.8 treats the residuals e_it(w) as fixed constants—valid for fixed augmentation/IPW, but the paper also demonstrates 'martingale violation' in Figure 5 using random augmentations for which formula (22) is not established; the impossibility claim for general data-dependent augmentations is not fully rigorous.

The asymptotic confidence sequences require V_t(w) → ∞ and inherit strong-approximation error terms; finite-sample behavior away from the asymptotic regime is not explored (the simulations use N=500 only), and no nonasymptotic (e.g., Hoeffding/empirical-Bernstein style) fallback is offered for small experiments.

The union-bound construction doubles the effective α per arm and the confidence process width grows with t rather than shrinking; while the paper argues practical conclusions are rescaling-invariant, the resulting procedure's finite-sample power loss relative to a joint (two-arm) boundary is not quantified.

Reproducibility is limited: the real telemetry case study uses proprietary data with no code release mentioned; the synthetic DGP is fully specified, but no artifact or implementation details (beyond boundary parameters) are provided.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work: the machinery (mixture boundaries, strong approximation, design-based confidence sequences) is largely imported from Ham et al. (2022), Howard et al. (2021), and Waudby-Smith et al. (2024); the core new elements are the delay-aware filtration characterization and the impossibility result, which, while correct, constitute a specialized contribution.

Minor presentation issues: the reliance on informal 'F_{t−}(w)' notation for left limits in a continuous-time setting, and some claims (e.g., 'strictly F_{t_{i(w)−}}(w)-measurable' for the running mean) would benefit from more precise statement; the dependence of the event-time augmentation on unobserved potential event times for the counterfactual arm deserves explicit discussion of why the estimator remains computable.
